title: Persia: The First World Empire

cards.h: A king who was told to be kind to conquered people
cards.b:
In 539 BCE, Cyrus the Great rode into Babylon, the biggest city in the world. The people did not fight him. Some cheered. How do you take a city without a war?

The answer says a lot about how the Persians built the largest empire the world had yet seen.

cards.h: From a small kingdom to everything
cards.b:
Cyrus came from Persis (today's Fars, Iran). Around 550 BCE he beat the Medes, then Lydia's rich king Croesus, then Babylon in 539 BCE. His son Cambyses added Egypt in 525 BCE.

This was the Achaemenid Empire, named after an ancestor, Achaemenes.

Darius I (ruled 522-486 BCE) split the empire into provinces run by governors called satraps. He built the Royal Road, about 2,500 km from Sardis to Susa, with relay stations for messengers. Standard coins and weights helped trade.

cards.h: A message carved on a cliff
cards.b:
At Behistun in Iran, Darius had a giant relief carved about 520 BCE. It tells how he won the throne, in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian.

In the 1800s, scholars such as Henry Rawlinson used it to decipher cuneiform, much like the Rosetta Stone did for hieroglyphs.

Persian kings let people keep their own religions and laws as long as they paid tribute. Cyrus is credited in the Bible (Book of Ezra) with letting Jews in Babylon return to Jerusalem.

They also worshipped Ahura Mazda. Their faith is often tied to the prophet Zoroaster, whose dates are very uncertain.

Persia clashed with Greek cities. At Marathon (490 BCE) Athens beat a Persian force. In 480 BCE Xerxes invaded with a huge army and fleet. The Greeks held at Thermopylae and then won at Salamis.

Persia remained powerful for another 150 years until Alexander arrived.

cards.h: Was the Cyrus Cylinder the first human rights charter?
cards.b:
The Cyrus Cylinder is a clay barrel, now in the British Museum. It says Cyrus restored gods to their temples and let displaced people go home.

Some call it the first charter of human rights. Many historians disagree. It was a standard royal boast written to win over Babylon. It shows good policy, but not modern rights. Historians argue about how to read it.

Persia reached the Indus. Around 518 BCE, Darius I took Gandhara and the Indus valley, and his inscriptions list Hindush as a province. Herodotus claims it paid the largest tribute of all, in gold dust.

Persian rule left real traces. The Kharosthi script of the north-west grew out of Aramaic, the empire's office script. Some historians see Persian echoes in Ashoka's habit of carving edicts on rock and in the polished stone of Mauryan pillars, though how much was borrowed is debated.

When Alexander later marched east, he was chasing the edges of this same empire into Punjab.

Five things to remember

  1. Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE.
  2. Darius built satrapies and the Royal Road.
  3. The Behistun inscription helped crack cuneiform.
  4. Persia ruled many peoples with tolerance and tribute.
  5. Gandhara and Sindh were Persian provinces.

Think about it

  • Is tolerance a smart strategy or a moral choice for an empire?
  • Why did a fast road matter for control?
